# Quirks Table

*Pages PDF 8-9*

## **Quirks Table**
As an option, the GM may decide to generate a quirk, something out of the ordinary. To work out a quirk, roll 2d10. If the tavern is a Silver Tier location, add 5 to the roll. If it is a Gold Tier location, add 10 to the roll. 

The GM should consider whether the quirk applies to the tavern — many of these quirks could have game-changing consequences, would not be suitable for isolated coaching inns, or may make the Characters’ stay here a little too distracting — so they should be handled with care and used with discretion. 

| 2d10 | Quirk |
|---|---|
| 3 | as the Brustellites of Altdorf, or the New Millennialists of Middenheim. The rally will be held in a private room and is initially quiet but grows rowdy as time passes. If the Characters investigate, they may be taken in as converts to the cause or be suspected of spying for the authorities. Hedge School.  The tavern is host to several amateur scholars and tradesmen who are willing to spend evenings |
| 4 | teaching skills and knowledge to the local community. This has a clear prosocial aspect and is generally to the benefit of participants. However, it may also indicate insularity, in that the local community wants to inculcate particular values in its members and avoid sharing wider knowledge and beliefs. Destruction.  The tavern is recovering after recent riotous behaviour. Many of the tables and bar stools have been |
| 5 | smashed and much of the stock has been stolen or ruined. The staff are worried that the landlord won’t be able to pay them. The landlord is worried that he will soon be out of business. Dues to Pay.  A protection racket is putting the squeeze on the landlord, or he is behind on his taxes. Prices are |
| 6 | inflated by up to 25% to ensure the gang boss, or the exciseman, gets his cut. Surprisingly Good Fare. |
| 7 | The tavern may treat itself as one Tier higher for the purposes of determining what sort of food and drink is available. |
| 8 | Shifty Customers.  This tavern is a haven to the underworld. Roll three times on the  Criminal Customer Table . Shrine.  There is a shrine to one of the gods at the tavern. It may be a small vestibule built into an outside wall or a |
| 9 | discrete room used by staff and travellers. The shrine is most likely dedicated to Sigmar, but may be to Ulric (in the north), Taal (in the wilds), Rhya (in the countryside), or Ranald (if the clientele includes thieves). Regular visitors to the tavern will tend to abide by the strictures associated with the god, even if they are not priests themselves. Dicing or Card Game Tournament.  Tonight the tavern will be playing host to a regular gaming event. This will |
| 10 | likely be Al-zahr or Scarlet Empress. There will be 2d10 extra customers present to take part in the games, and the usual stakes will be doubled. Low on Stock.  Due to a missed delivery, or bad batch of brew, the Landlord is down to his last 2d10 pints of ale. 11–12 He may be honest about the shortfall, or watering down the remaining drink in the hope that no one will notice. Boycott.  The Characters may be surprised to find that they are the only people patronising the tavern. The |
| 13 | landlord has done something to offend the locals, such as holding unpopular religious or political opinions. The tavern staff will be happy to wait on the Characters, but if the Characters stay at the tavern, they may find themselves judged guilty by association. Provocateurs.  A group of three young men are trying to make life very hard for the staff of the tavern. They demand immediate service, then complain about it once it is offered. They talk loudly and charmlessly to other |
| 14 | customers but take offence at the slightest insult. They sing loud and tuneless ditties. Their behaviour is extremely off-putting but stops short of any bannable offence. In fact, they have been paid by the proprietor of a rival tavern to make coming here a miserable experience. |

| 2d10 | Quirk |
|---|---|
| 15 | Short-Staffed.  Several staff are currently ill or away without leave. The tavern counts as having a Skeleton Staff. Secret Agent. |
| 16 | One of the customers is a spy. They may be employed by a local authority to keep an ear out for news of revolution or criminal activity, or by a foreign power to learn of interesting local developments. Unusual Pet.  The tavern keeps an unusual aniumal as a mascot, such as Beaky the Pelican at the Pelican’s Perch |
| 17 | in Marienburg. The owners and regulars will indulge this creature and put up with it upsetting drinks or stealing food, but stangers may find it an unwelcome annoyance. |
| 18 | Exotic Quirk.  Something uncanny, fantastical, or monstrous. Roll again on the  Exotic Quirk Table . |
| 19 | No Food.  The landlord is waiting on supplies and desperately apologising to disappointed customers. Poor Quality Food.  Whilst the food served here may usually be decent, or even fine, the landlord has saved |
| 20–21 | money on some Poor Quality ingredients. Customers eating the food will notice it is spiced with more salt, pepper, and herbs than usual on an  Easy (+40) Perception (Taste)  Test. Rats in the Walls.  The tavern is suffering from a serious rat infestation. They may spoil food and disturb the rest |
| 21 | of sleepers by scampering about after dark. The landlord may be trying to keep the fact of the infestation a secret, but will be desperate to secure the services of a good Rat Catcher. Superstitious Landlord.  The landlord has a pronounced superstition, maybe because of their Dooming (they may not abide the sound of a drum), a religious belief (they might not tolerate rudeness towards Dwarfs), or |
| 22 | something picked up from life at sea (they may hate whistling unless there is no wind). They will take umbrage at any customer they regard as tempting fate, and will ban repeat offenders. You’re Barred! |
| 23 | The landlord keeps a strict blacklist of banned customers and is quick to add to it in the case of rude or troublesome people. Surprisingly Poor Fare. |
| 24 | The tavern may treat itself as one Tier lower for the purposes of determining what sort of food and drink is available. |
| 25 | Special Offers.  To drum up some extra custom and get the tavern’s name spread about, the landlord is offering some amazing cut-price deals. Drinks and fare are currently half their normal price. Esoteric Club.  Once a week, a group with a specific and narrow field of interest meets at the tavern to discuss developments in their field. This may be the academic study of magical innovation, an obscure religious belief, an |
| 26 | interest in the history of a foreign nation or monstrous species, the latest discoveries from Lustria, or a similar niche interest. Whilst not unpleasant, these folk will quickly become irritated by anyone who distracts them from their discussion. Trapped Treasures.  The owner of the tavern has gone to great expense to ensure that the walls are hung with expensive artworks and silver decorations. Anticipating that a thief will one day help themselves to these prizes, |
| 27 | he has secreted poisoned needles behind some of the mountings. A character taking a trapped piece from the wall must pass a  Challenging (+0) Sleight of Hand  Test or be stabbed by a needle, and must pass a  Hard (–20) Endurance  Test or gain 1  Poisoned  Condition, plus a further 1  Poisoned  Condition per –SL. |
| 28 | Alvatafl Tournament.  Tonight, the tavern will be playing host to a regular gaming event. This will likely be Alvatafl. There will be 2d10 extra customers present to take part in the games. Stakes begin at 3 GC per game. Unsuitable Staff.  Whether a result of incompetence or poor morale, the staff seemed comically unsuited to their |
| 29 | jobs. The cook fries lobster and boils venison, the servants swear like sailors, the doorman is craven and puny, and the proprietor seems permanently on the verge of a nervous breakdown. Who Let Them In?  Rough folk who look most out of place. Roll 1d10 on the  Customer Table . If this results in |
| 30 | a criminal or exotic customer, roll 2d10 on the respective table. These folk may have a reasonable excuse for being here, or they may have simply wandered in whilst the doorman was dozing. |
